If \(n=1\), the factorization has empty transvection lists and no \(2\times2\) blocks; the determinant-square hypothesis gives exactly the chosen-line square scaling. Assume now that \(n\ge2\). The classical transvection reduction for invertible matrices in dimension at least $2$~\cite[Ch.~IV]{Artin1957GeometricAlgebra} writes $g$ as basis transvections, a diagonal basis scaling, and basis transvections. Because $\det(g)$ is a square, the middle diagonal factor has square total determinant.
